nodes.title: Continual Learning Model with Dynamic Adaptation and Flexibility for Incremental Classes
nodes.authors: Minami Hotta; Noriko Ogasawara; Kengo Miyajima; Ryotaro Shimizu; Masayuki Goto
nodes.institutions: Waseda University
nodes.keywords: continual learning; class-incremental learning; few-shot learning; facts; embedding space; semantic diversity; covariance matrix; image classification
nodes.abstract: In recent years, deep learning models have achieved highly accurate image classification. However, in scenarios where the number of target classes continues to increase while using a model, it is not very effective to retrain the model by using all data from the beginning each time. Consequently, there has been increasing interest in class-incremental learning, which sequentially updates existing models with newly introduced classes. In particular, Forward Compatible Few-Shot Class-Incremental Learning (FACT) has demonstrated high classification performance by proactively reserving regions within the embedding space to represent knowledge of classes that will be added in the future. In this study, we propose FACT+, which seeks to further enhance the performance of FACT by incorporating two key extensions. First, to account for the semantic diversity (i.e., the breadth or narrowness of meaning) of each class, we introduce variability into each class’s covariance matrix. Second, to address the issue of insufficient learning from incremental data, we implement a mechanism to continuously update the model’s knowledge through the reuse of data collected during deployment. Experimental results show that the proposed method outperforms FACT in terms of classification accuracy and confirm the validity of the embedding space learned by the proposed approach.

nodes.title: Auditing Political Bias in Text Generation by GPT-4 using Sociocultural and Demographic Personas: Case of Bengali Ethnolinguistic Communities
nodes.authors: Dipto Das; Syed Ishtiaque Ahmed; Shion Guha
nodes.institutions: University of Toronto
nodes.primary_topic: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI
nodes.keywords: political bias; GPT-4; Bengali language; large language models; low-resource languages; personas; political orientation; religious identity; national identity; sociocultural identity; multilingual models; text generation
nodes.abstract: Though large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in multilingual contexts, their political and sociocultural biases in lowresource languages remain critically underexplored.In this paper, we investigate how LLM-generated texts in Bengali shift in response to personas with varying political orientations (left vs. right), religious identities (Hindu vs. Muslim), and national affiliations (Bangladeshi vs. Indian).In a quasiexperimental study, we simulate these personas and prompt an LLM to respond to political discussions.Measuring the shifts relative to responses for a baseline Bengali persona, we examined how political orientation influences LLM outputs, how topical association shapes the political leanings of outputs, and how demographic persona-induced changes align with differently politically oriented variations.Our findings highlight leftleaning political bias in Bengali text generation and its significant association with Muslim sociocultural and demographic identity.We also connect our findings with broader discussions around emancipatory politics, epistemological considerations, and alignment of multilingual models.

nodes.title: How Effectively Can BERT Models Interpret Context and Detect Bengali Communal Violent Text?
nodes.authors: Abdullah Khondoker; Enam Ahmed Taufik; Md Iftekhar Islam Tashik; Shaiful Mahmud; Farig Sadeque
nodes.institutions: BRAC University
nodes.keywords: Bengali text; BanglaBERT; social media; ensemble learning; class imbalance; LIME explainability; contextual understanding; religious conflict
nodes.abstract: The spread of cyber hatred has led to communal violence, fueling aggression and conflicts between various religious, ethnic, and social groups, posing a significant threat to social harmony. Despite its critical importance, the classification of communal violent text remains an underexplored area in existing research. This study aims to enhance the accuracy of detecting text that incites communal violence, focusing specifically on Bengali textual data sourced from social media platforms. We introduce a fine-tuned BanglaBERT model tailored for this task, achieving a macro F1 score of 0.60. To address the issue of data imbalance, our dataset was expanded by adding 1,794 instances, which facilitated the development and evaluation of a fine-tuned ensemble model. This ensemble model demonstrated an improved performance, achieving a macro F1 score of 0.63, thus highlighting its effectiveness in this domain. In addition to quantitative performance metrics, qualitative analysis revealed instances where the models struggled with context understanding, leading to occasional misclassifications, even when predictions were made with high confidence. Through analyzing the cosine similarity between words, we identified certain limitations in the pre-trained BanglaBERT models, particularly in their ability to distinguish between closely related communal and non-communal terms. To further interpret the model's decisions, we applied LIME, which helped to uncover specific areas where the model struggled in understanding context, contributing to errors in classification. These findings highlight the promise of NLP and interpretability tools in reducing online communal violence. Our work contributes to the growing body of research in communal violence detection and offers a foundation for future studies aiming to refine these techniques for better accuracy and societal impact.

nodes.title: Bengali Cyberbullying: Detection, Categorization, and Gender Bias Analysis
nodes.venue: IEEE ... International Conference on Data Mining workshops
nodes.authors: Md. Mithun Hossain; Md. Shakil Hossain; Sudipto Chaki; Md. Saifur Rahman; Mohammad Ali Moni
nodes.institutions: Bangladesh University of Business and Technology; Charles Sturt University
nodes.keywords: cyberbullying; Bengali language; cyberbullying detection; multi-task learning; transformer models; social media text; low-resource languages
nodes.abstract: Cyberbullying has spread like wildfire on social media, seriously harming people’s emotional and physical health. Because of linguistic and cultural differences, addressing this issue in Bengali poses particular difficulties. By emphasizing three crucial tasks—detection, classification, and gender bias analysis—this study offers a thorough strategy to combat cyberbullying in Bengali. To handle multiple tasks concurrently, we provide a unique multi-task learning framework based on a Transformer-based model. The process involves pre-trained tokenization, augmentation, and data cleaning to guarantee that the supplied data is relevant and of high quality. We assess our approach to the investigation of gender bias, the classification of cyberbullying categories, and the identification of particular bullying labels. The Transformer model outperforms baseline models like Bi-LSTM, Bi-GRU, and CNN, with Macro F1 scores of 97.73% for gender classification, 95.31% for categorization, and 98.61% for bullying label detection. These findings demonstrate the model’s efficacy in identifying nuanced linguistic patterns and offer a solid remedy for Bengali cyberbullying analysis, demonstrating its capacity to manage complex text data effectively.

nodes.title: Multi-Source Bangla Violence Text Dataset and Transformer-Based Stacking Ensemble for Social Media Content Moderation
nodes.venue: International Conference on Power, Electronics, Communications, Computing, and Intelligent Infrastructure (PECCII)
nodes.authors: Maliha Rahman Moon; Md. Siam; Asmita Hoque Pospita; Hrithik Majumdar Shibu
nodes.institutions: R. P. Shaha University; University of Essex
nodes.keywords: violence detection; Bengali language; social media content moderation; stacking ensemble; BanglaBERT; XLM-R; low-resource languages; YouTube; Facebook; TikTok; text classification
nodes.abstract: The exponential rise in user-generated content on platforms like Facebook, YouTube, and TikTok has led to a surge in violence-inciting language, particularly in low-resource languages like Bangla. This highlights the urgent need for effective automated systems capable of detecting and filtering harmful content to ensure safer digital environments. In this study, we propose the BX Stacking Ensemble Model, a novel approach combining the strengths of two powerful transformer-based models, BanglaBERT and XLM-RoBERTa, to enhance the detection of violence-related text in Bangla. The model is trained on a newly compiled dataset of 11,933 samples, which integrates the Vio-Lens dataset with 5,887 additional instances from YouTube, Facebook, and TikTok. The dataset is carefully annotated into three categories: Non-Violence, Passive Violence, and Active Violence, capturing a wide range of violence-related expressions. Alongside the ensemble model, we also evaluate two additional approaches: Linguistic Features with Traditional Machine Learning Models, using TF-IDF for text representation, and Transformer-Based Models, such as BanglaBERT and XLM-RoBERTa. By comparing these methods, we demonstrate that the BX Stacking Ensemble Model significantly outperforms baseline models, achieving a Macro F1 score of 0.85. The results underscore the effectiveness of combining language-specific and multilingual transformers, providing a scalable solution for real world content moderation. This research contributes to safer digital communication in Bengali-speaking communities and illustrates the potential of ensemble learning techniques for complex text classification tasks in content moderation.

nodes.title: Transformers for Low-Resource Religious Hate Speech Detection: A Comparative Study on Bangla Social Media Discourse
nodes.venue: IEEE/WIC/ACM International Conference on Web Intelligence and Intelligent Agent Technology (WI-IAT)
nodes.authors: Ashiqur Rahman Saron; Hasin Almas Sifat; Mahin Montasir Afif; Md. Mortuza Ahmmed; M. Mostafizur Rahman; Mufti Mahmud
nodes.institutions: American International University-Bangladesh; King Fahd University of Petroleum and Minerals
nodes.keywords: Bengali language; low-resource languages; transformer models; DistilBERT; XLNet; Electra; social media comments; content moderation; cross-lingual transfer learning; domain-adaptive pretraining
nodes.abstract: Religious hate speech detection in the web for low-resource languages like Bangla presents significant challenges due to linguistic complexity and socio-cultural nuances. This study evaluates the effectiveness of six transformer-based models on a Bangla religious hate speech dataset sourced from social media comments targeting Hindu and Muslim communities in Bangladesh and India. Among the models tested, DistilBERT, XLNet, and ELECTRA demonstrated superior performance. DistilBERT achieved the highest overall accuracy of approximately 91.7%, along with a strong F1 score close to 92%, supported by an impressive recall of over 95% and a ROC AUC of 0.98. XLNet showed outstanding precision at 98% and a ROC AUC of 0.979, while ELECTRA balanced precision and recall effectively, delivering around 91.5% accuracy and a comparable F1 score. These results highlight the potential of transformer architectures to advance hate speech detection in low-resource languages such as Bangla, offering promising foundations for automated content moderation tools that can help mitigate online religious intolerance. Future work will focus on improving model robustness through domain-adaptive pretraining, exploring cross-lingual transfer learning to extend capabilities to other South Asian low-resource languages and developing scalable real-time moderation frameworks for practical deployment in social media platforms.

nodes.title: BanglaHateCorpus: A large-scale bangla benchmark for hate speech classification and a transformer-based deep learning method
nodes.authors: Anika Tasnim Rodela; Mahbub E. Sobhani; Sakif Naieb Raiyan; Mohammad Nurul Huda; Dewan Md. Farid
nodes.institutions: BRAC University; Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology; Bangladesh University of Professionals; Southeast University; United International University
nodes.keywords: hate speech detection; Bengali language; mixture of experts; low-resource languages; social media; annotated corpus; LLM-assisted annotation; parameter-efficient models
nodes.abstract: Hate speech on social media refers to content that threatens, attacks, or dehumanizes people or groups based on specified characteristics, thereby eroding trust, worsening societal divisions, and causing psychological harm to the targeted communities. In digitally connected South Asian societies, strong in-group bonds and online inter-group hatred can rapidly lead to real-world violence, a risk intensified by the proliferation of Bangla texts, highlighting the urgent need for robust detection in this low-resource language. Previous studies have mostly focused on building their datasets by scraping various sources, without emphasizing standardized quality annotation or ensuring classification accuracy. To address these gaps, we introduce BanglaHateCorpus, a unified corpus of 168K examples consolidated from eight public sources, rigorously de-duplicated and annotated through a two-stage, human and LLM-assisted pipeline. Building on this benchmark, we propose BanHateFormer, a novel deep-learning model that embodies state-of-the-art transformer components, and replaces the conventional feed-forward blocks with a Mixture-of-Experts layer followed by a binary classification head. BanHateFormer achieves state-of-the-art classification results, as assessed by accuracy, precision, recall, and macro F1-score with approximately 94.74 times fewer parameters than comparable models, achieving a 91.33% macro F1-score on the BanglaHateCorpus dataset and 78.96% on the transliterated BanTH benchmark. BanHateFormer outperforms BanglaBERT and XLM-RoBERTa by up to 2.57% with three times fewer parameters, and improves macro F1-score by 3.38% on transliterated text, demonstrating strong performance on romanized inputs. BanHateFormer significantly surpasses existing transformer-based models in balancing memory efficiency and high-fidelity outputs, marking a breakthrough in hate speech classification with optimal space utilization.

nodes.title: MARS2 2025 Challenge on Multimodal Reasoning: Datasets, Methods, Results, Discussion, and Outlook
nodes.venue: IEEE International Conference on Computer Vision Workshops
nodes.authors: Peng Xu; Shengwu Xiong; Jiajun Zhang; Yaxiong Chen; Bowen Zhou; Chen Change Loy; David A. Clifton; Kyoung Mu Lee; Luc Van Gool; Ruiming He; Ruilin Yao; Xinwei Long; Jirui Huang; Kai Tian; Sa Yangbcd; Yihua Shao; Jin Feng; Yue Zhong; Jiakai Zhou; Cheng Tang; Tianyu Zou; Yifang Zhang; Junming Liang; Guoyou Li; Zhaoxiang Wang; Qiang Zhou; Yichen Zhao; Shili Xiong; Hyeongjin Nam; Jaerin Lee; Jaeyoung Chung; JoonKyu Park; Junghun Oh; Kanggeon Lee; Wooseok Lee; Juneyoung Ro; Turghun Osman; Can Hu; Chaoyang Liao; Cheng Chen; Chengcheng Han; Chenhao Qiu; Chong Peng; Cong Xu; Dailin Lid; Feiyu Wang; Feng Gao; Guibo Zhu; Guopeng Tang; Haibo Lu; Han Fang; Han Qi; Hanxiao Wu; Haobo Cheng; Hongbo Sun; Hongyao Chen; Huayong Hu; Hui Lid; Jiaheng Mad; Jiang Yu; Jianing Wang; Jie Yang; Jing He; Jinglin Zhou; Jingxuan Lid; Josef Kittler; Lihao Zheng; Linnan Zhao; Mengxi Jia; Muyang Yan; Nguyen Thanh Thien; Pu Luo; Qi Lid; Shien Song; Shijie Dong; Shuai Shao; Shutao Lid; Taofeng Xue; Tianyang Xu; Tianyi Gao; Tingting Lid; Wei Zhang; Weiyang Su; Xiaodong Dong; Xiao-Jun Wu; Xiaopeng Zhou; Xin Chen; Xin Wei; Xinyi You; Xudong Kang; Xujie Zhou; Xusheng Liu; Yanan Wang; Yanbin Huang; Yang Liu; Yang Yang; Yanglin Deng; Yashu Kang; Ye Yuan; Yi Wen
nodes.keywords: multimodal reasoning; multimodal large language models; benchmark; visual grounding; visual question answering; spatial awareness; visual reasoning
nodes.abstract: This paper reviews the MARS2 2025 Challenge on Multi-modal Reasoning. We aim to bring together different approaches in multimodal machine learning and LLMs via a large benchmark. We hope it better allows researchers to follow the state-of-the-art in this very dynamic area. Mean-while, a growing number of testbeds have boosted the evolution of general-purpose large language models. Thus, this year's MARS2 focuses on real-world and specialized scenarios to broaden the multimodal reasoning applications of MLLMs. Our organizing team released two tailored datasets Lens and AdsQA as test sets, which support general reasoning in 12 daily scenarios and domain-specific reasoning in advertisement videos, respectively. We evaluated 40+ baselines that include both generalist MLLMs and task-specific models, and opened up three competition tracks, i.e., Visual Grounding in Real-world Scenarios (VGRS), Visual Question Answering with Spatial Awareness (VQA-SA), and Visual Reasoning in Creative Advertisement Videos (VR-Ads). Finally, 76 teams from the renowned academic and industrial institutions have registered and 40+ valid submissions (out of 1200+) have been included in our ranking lists. Our datasets, code sets (40+ base-lines and 15+ participants' methods), and rankings are publicly available on the MARS2 workshop website and our GitHub organization page https://github.com/mars2workshop/, where our updates and announcements of upcoming events will be continuously provided.

nodes.title: Object-Uni: A Unified Model for Object-Centric Spatial Understanding and Controllable Generation
nodes.authors: Mining Tan; Yinuo Wang; Ziqi Zhou; Weize Quan; Sifei Li; Jingdong Chen; Dandan Zheng; Libin Wang; Weiming Dong
nodes.institutions: Ant Group (China); Chinese Academy of Sciences; Institute of Automation; Tsinghua University; University of Chinese Academy of Sciences
nodes.keywords: object pose estimation; novel view synthesis; multimodal large language models; spatial reasoning
nodes.abstract: Unified models for visual understanding and generation have made rapid progress, yet they still lack the ability to understand and manipulate the spatial states of object instances. Existing models can describe objects in natural language, but they struggle to precisely represent continuous object poses and generate geometrically consistent images under target viewpoints. To mitigate this, we propose \emph{Object-Uni}, a unified model for object-centric spatial understanding and controllable generation. Specifically, we formulate object-centric spatial intelligence as a unified problem connecting pose perception, spatial reasoning, pose-conditioned generation, and object-centric novel view synthesis. We treat object pose as an explicit geometric variable shared by understanding and generation, rather than merely a prediction label or control signal. To make pose usable by multimodal large language models, we propose a viewpoint-based orientation abstraction that maps orientation into structured viewpoint descriptions while preserving continuous geometric supervision. We further construct an object-centric spatial benchmark (UniSpatial-80K) and train a unified model with an object-token-grounded pose anchor to associate each instance with its pose state. Experiments show that our model improves object-level pose understanding and pose-controllable generation, moving unified models from describing objects toward manipulating spatial states.

nodes.title: Why MLLMs Struggle to Determine Object Orientations
nodes.authors: Anju Gopinath; Nikhil Krishnaswamy; Bruce A. Draper
nodes.institutions: Colorado State University
nodes.keywords: multimodal large language models; object orientation; rotation sensing; CLIP; SigLIP; ViT; LLaVA; Qwen2.5-VL; image-text alignment
nodes.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) struggle with tasks that require reasoning about 2D object orientation in images, as documented in prior work. Tong et al. and Nichols et al. hypothesize that these failures originate in the visual encoder, since commonly used encoders such as CLIP and SigLIP are trained for image-text semantic alignment rather than geometric reasoning. We design a controlled empirical protocol to test this claim by measuring whether rotations can be recovered from encoder representations. In particular, we examine SigLIP and ViT features from LLaVA OneVision and Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct models, respectively, using full images, and examine CLIP representations in LLaVA 1.5 and 1.6 using rotated foreground patches against natural background images. Our null hypothesis is that orientation information is not preserved in the encoder embeddings and we test this by training linear regressors to predict object orientation from encoded features. Contrary to the hypothesis, we find that orientation information is recoverable from encoder representations: simple linear models accurately predict object orientations from embeddings. This contradicts the assumption that MLLM orientation failures originate in the visual encoder. Having rejected the accepted hypothesis that MLLMs struggle with 2D orientation tasks because of visual encoder limitations, we still don't know why they fail. Although a full explanation is beyond the scope of this paper, we show that although present, orientation information is spread diffusely across tens of thousands of features. This may or may not be while MLLMs fail to exploit the available orientation information.

nodes.title: WildRoadBench: A Wild Aerial Road-Damage Grounding Benchmark for Vision-Language Models and Autonomous Agents
nodes.authors: Bingnan Liu; Chenhang Cui; Rui Huang; Jiani Luo; Zhirong Shen; Tinghao Wang; Xiande Huang; Lingbei Meng; Fei Shen; An Zhang
nodes.institutions: National University of Singapore; University of Electronic Science and Technology of China; University of Science and Technology of China
nodes.keywords: visual grounding; road damage detection; aerial imagery; UAV imagery; vision-language models; LLM agents; autonomous agents; benchmark; open-source models; image annotation
nodes.abstract: We introduce WildRoadBench, a wild aerial road-damage grounding benchmark that couples direct visual grounding by vision-language models with autonomous research-and-engineering by LLM-driven agents on a single professionally annotated UAV corpus. The same image set and the same per-class AP_50 metric are evaluated under two protocols. The VLM Track measures whether a fixed VLM can localise domain-specific damage from one image and one short prompt under a unified prompting, decoding and parsing pipeline. The Agent Track measures whether an autonomous agent, given only a written task brief, a small exploratory slice and a fixed interaction budget, can search the public web, adapt pretrained components, write training and inference code, and submit predictions through a scalar-feedback oracle on a hidden holdout. We benchmark a broad pool of closed-source frontier models and open-source VLMs together with several frontier LLM-driven agents. Both routes remain far from reliable performance in this wild setting: closed-source frontier models lead the VLM leaderboard but still leave more than half of the metric on the table; open-source grounders plateau well below them, and newer generations or reasoning-style variants do not consistently improve grounding; small targets collapse for every open-source model; agents lag the strongest VLM despite richer affordances, and several fail to land a valid submission within the budget. We release the code and data at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/wildroadbench-0607 to support reproducible follow-up research.

nodes.title: Autoregressive Mosaics: Probing 2D Spatial Reasoning in Text-Only Language Models
nodes.authors: Ashwin Nedungadi; Stefan Oehmcke; Stefan Lüdtke
nodes.institutions: University of Rostock
nodes.keywords: text-to-image generation; layout generation; code generation; SVG; geometric reasoning
nodes.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) trained only on text and code can sometimes generate programs that draw recognizable images. However, it is unclear whether this reflects an internal representation of 2D spatial layout or simply the ability to translate spatial descriptions into code. We introduce Autoregressive Mosaics (AM-Bench), a benchmark that separates these factors: First, a translation task gives a model a fully specified geometry of a picture in words as a prompt and asks for the code that produces it. Second, a layout task requires the model to compose an image from an underspecified prompt. Across eight open-weight text-and-code-only models, all models reliably translate specified geometry into code, but their open-ended layout performance differs substantially, indicating that these differences are not explained by code-generation ability alone. An output-medium ablation further shows that the interface or medium of expression that the model uses matters: replacing procedural code with raw SVG improves layout scores across all models. Finally, probing model activations shows that a coarse layout plan is present before generation, but reflects only the layout implied by the prompt. During generation, models track the evolving geometric state instead of executing an initially fixed plan. Overall, these results show that 2D spatial performance in text-only LLMs depends on both the model and the output medium, and is not explained by code-generation ability alone.

nodes.authors: Dana Serditova; Kevin Tang
nodes.institutions: Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf; University of Florida; University of Regensburg
nodes.keywords: Tyneside English; dialect variation; phonetic variation; transcription errors; phonological variation; glottalization; vowel quality; socioeconomic status; gender differences; age differences; acoustic phonetics

nodes.title: Benchmarking Bengali Dialectal Bias: A Multi-Stage Framework Integrating RAG-Based Translation and Human-Augmented RLAIF
nodes.venue: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP)
nodes.authors: K. M. Jubair Sami; Dipto Sumit; Ariyan Hossain; Farig Sadeque
nodes.institutions: BRAC University
nodes.keywords: Bengali dialects; low-resource languages; retrieval-augmented generation; question translation; LLM-as-a-judge; translation quality assessment; question answering; benchmark dataset; language divergence; model scale
nodes.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) frequently exhibit performance biases against regional dialects of low-resource languages.However, frameworks to quantify these disparities remain scarce.We propose a two-phase framework to evaluate dialectal bias, operationalized as comprehension degradation relative to standard Bengali, in LLM question-answering across nine Bengali dialects.First, we translate and gold-label standard Bengali questions into dialectal variants adopting a retrievalaugmented generation (RAG) pipeline to prepare 4,000 question sets.Since traditional translation quality evaluation metrics fail on unstandardized dialects, we evaluate fidelity using an LLM-as-a-judge, which human correlation confirms outperforms legacy metrics.Second, we benchmark 19 LLMs across these gold-labeled sets, running 68,395 RLAIF evaluations validated through multi-judge agreement and human fallback.Our findings reveal severe performance drops linked to linguistic divergence.For instance, responses to the highly divergent Chittagong dialect score 5.44/10, compared to 7.68/10 for Tangail.Furthermore, increased model scale does not consistently mitigate this bias.We contribute a validated translation quality evaluation method, a rigorous benchmark dataset, and a Critical Bias Sensitivity (CBS) metric for safety-critical applications.

nodes.title: "It Would Make a Geordie Feel at Home": Regional Accent Perceptions and Speech Accommodation in Voice AI
nodes.authors: Dana Serditova; Kevin Tang; Jochen Steffens
nodes.institutions: Hochschule Düsseldorf University of Applied Sciences; University of Regensburg
nodes.keywords: voice assistants; regional accents; speech accommodation; speech recognition; synthetic speech; Standard Southern British English; user perceptions of AI; inclusive technology design; human-AI interaction; social stereotypes
nodes.abstract: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems often perform less accurately for speakers of regional dialects, but less is known about how users respond to these limitations and how regional voices produced by voice assistants (VAs) are evaluated through a sociolinguistic lens. This study investigates these issues among speakers of Newcastle English (Geordies), examining both linguistic accommodation to voice technologies and perceptions of regional versus mainstream-accented VA voices. Participants interacted with a simulated VA that spoke either Newcastle English or Standard Southern British English (SSBE). They subsequently completed semi-structured interviews about their experiences with the experimental VA and voice technologies, language use, accent attitudes, and place orientation. The findings reveal a two-way process of sociolinguistic bias. The Geordie VA was associated with familiarity, warmth, personality, and local belonging, but also with concerns about professionalism and authority, whereas the SSBE voice was perceived as more neutral, clear, and credible. Participants also reported adapting their speech when voice technologies failed to recognise them, most commonly by shifting to a more mainstream accent, enunciating more clearly, and speaking more slowly. These strategies are similar to accommodation in human-human interaction and reflect users' perceptions of what technologies can recognise, also known as perceived intelligibility pressures. Overall, the findings demonstrate that voice technologies can reproduce existing accent biases both by encouraging users to suppress regional features and by activating established social stereotypes through synthetic voices. The study positions sociolinguistics as a bridge between understanding human-AI interaction and designing inclusive technologies around users' own linguistic priorities.

nodes.title: Meaning Over Morphology: A Multi-Metric Benchmark of LLMs for Bangla Dialect Translation
nodes.authors: Soumik Deb Niloy; S M Asif Ur Rahman; Mahbub E. Sobhani; Md. Golam Rabiul Alam; Farig Sadeque; Md. Rezuwan Hassan
nodes.institutions: BRAC University; United International University
nodes.keywords: low-resource languages; open-source large language models; multi-metric evaluation; semantic evaluation; translation benchmark
nodes.abstract: Regional dialects of Bangla, such as Sylheti and Chittagonian, pose significant challenges for natural language processing due to their low-resource nature and substantial linguistic variation from standard Bangla.In this work, we present a systematic evaluation of eight open-source LLMs for translating fifteen distinct Bangla dialects into standard Bangla.To achieve this comprehensive coverage, we utilize a combination of established benchmarks and a novel dataset curated from an ongoing regional linguistic project.We assess model performance using a multi-metric framework that combines exact-match and error-rate evaluations such as, Averaged BLEU, WER, and CER with embedding-based semantic metrics including BERTScore, METEOR, and COMET.Additionally, we perform a detailed dialect-level linguistic analysis to identify the deep-seated structural, orthographic, and semantic barriers inherent to dialectal translation.Our study highlights the strengths and limitations of current open-source models, provides empirical insights for future dialect-aware fine-tuning, and contributes a reproducible benchmark for the research community.

nodes.title: Digital Health Interventions in Dengue Surveillance to Detect and Predict Outbreak: A Scoping Review
nodes.authors: Marko Ferdian Salim; Tri Baskoro Tunggul Satoto; Danardono Danardono; D. Daniel
nodes.institutions: Universitas Gadjah Mada
nodes.keywords: dengue surveillance; digital health interventions; epidemic forecasting; geographic information systems; machine learning; social media; mobile application; Google Trends; web application; integrated surveillance systems
nodes.abstract: Background Dengue fever is a global concern, with half of the population at risk. Digital Health Interventions (DHIs) have been widely used in Dengue surveillance. Objective The objective of this review is to identify DHIs that have been used in Dengue surveillance. Methods A systematic literature search was performed on three primary databases: PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar. A total of 2637 studies, including duplicates, were found to be possibly pertinent to the study topic during the electronic search for the systematic literature review. After the screening of titles and abstracts, 51 studies remained eligible. Results The study analyzed 13 main categories of DHIs in Dengue surveillance, with Brazil, India, Sri Lanka, China, and Indonesia being the top five countries. Geographic Information System was the most used DHIs, followed by Machine Learning, Social Media, Mobile Applications, Google Trends, and Web Applications. DHIs were integrated, as evidenced by the deployment of many DHIs simultaneously in a single Dengue surveillance program. Conclusion Future research should concentrate on finding more efficient ways to combine all available data sources and approaches to improve data completeness and predictive model precision and identify Dengue outbreaks early.

nodes.title: Exploring the Scope and Potential of Local Newspaper-based Dengue Surveillance in Bangladesh
nodes.authors: Nazia Tasnim; Md. Istiak Hossain Shihab; M. Shahidur Rahman; Sheikh Rabiul Islam; Mohammad Ruhul Amin
nodes.institutions: Fordham University; Shahjalal University of Science and Technology; University of Hartford
nodes.keywords: dengue surveillance; local newspapers; news content analysis; news classification; human-in-the-loop annotation; Bangladesh
nodes.abstract: Dengue fever has been considered to be one of the global public health problems of the twenty-first century, especially in tropical and subtropical countries of the global south. The high morbidity and mortality rates of Dengue fever impose a huge economic and health burden for middle and low-income countries. It is so prevalent in such regions that enforcing a granular level of surveillance is quite impossible. Therefore, it is crucial to explore an alternative cost-effective solution that can provide updates of the ongoing situation in a timely manner. In this paper, we explore the scope and potential of a local newspaper-based dengue surveillance system, using well-known data-mining techniques, in Bangladesh from the analysis of the news contents written in the native language. In addition, we explain the working procedure of developing a novel database, using human-in-the-loop technique, for further analysis, and classification of dengue and its intervention-related news. Our classification method has an f-score of 91.45%, and matches the ground truth of reported cases quite closely. Based on the dengue and intervention-related news, we identified the regions where more intervention efforts are needed to reduce the rate of dengue infection. A demo of this project can be accessed at: http://erdos.dsm.fordham.edu:3009/

nodes.keywords: riddles; benchmark; large language models; cultural understanding; abductive reasoning; compositional reasoning; cross-lingual evaluation; human evaluation
nodes.abstract: As LLMs expand their language coverage, evaluating how well they understand and represent diverse cultures becomes increasingly important. However, many benchmarks remain English-centric, with limited cultural coverage and a focus on factual knowledge over its application in real-world cultural contexts. We propose CulturalRiddles, a benchmark of original, culturally grounded riddles created entirely by humans through a participatory community effort, spanning 62 cultures (45 countries, 51 languages). These riddles are deeply rooted in their respective cultures and require abductive and compositional reasoning, alongside detailed factual and social knowledge, language skills, and an understanding of culturally specific associations. We benchmark 28 LLM configurations using both automatic and large-scale human evaluation. Even frontier models achieve at most 22% accuracy in some communities. We publicly release all artifacts alongside an open contribution process to expand the benchmark's linguistic and cultural coverage.

nodes.title: Mitigating Task-Order Sensitivity and Forgetting via Hierarchical Second-Order Consolidation
nodes.authors: Protik Nag; Krishnan Raghavan; Vignesh Narayanan
nodes.keywords: continual learning; forgetting; Hessian regularization; Taylor series expansion; task sequencing; knowledge integration
nodes.abstract: We introduce $\textbf{Hierarchical Taylor Series-based Continual Learning (HTCL)}$, a framework that couples fast local adaptation with conservative, second-order global consolidation to address the high variance introduced by random task ordering. To address task-order effects, HTCL identifies the best intra-group task sequence and integrates the resulting local updates through a Hessian-regularized Taylor expansion, yielding a consolidation step with theoretical guarantees. The approach naturally extends to an $L$-level hierarchy, enabling multiscale knowledge integration in a manner not supported by conventional single-level CL systems. Across a wide range of datasets and replay and regularization baselines, HTCL acts as a model-agnostic consolidation layer that consistently enhances performance, yielding mean accuracy gains of $7\%$ to $25\%$ while reducing the standard deviation of final accuracy by up to $68\%$ across random task permutations.

nodes.title: Bengali Descriptive Symptom to Disease Prediction Using Machine Learning for Improved Healthcare
nodes.venue: IEEE International Conference on Quantum Photonics, Artificial Intelligence & Networking (QPAIN)
nodes.authors: Sahela Rahman; Md. Shahid Uz Zaman
nodes.institutions: Rajshahi University of Engineering and Technology
nodes.keywords: Bengali language; symptom-based disease prediction; automated diagnosis; TF-IDF vectorization; random forest
nodes.abstract: In linguistically varied regions like Bangladesh, the capacity to predict diseases based on patient-reported symptoms is a crucial aspect of healthcare. However, modern automated diagnostic tools often do not support Bengali, which puts native speakers at a disadvantage. Our study focuses on machine learning approaches that utilize 141 samples of Bengali symptom descriptions for each of the 65 distinct diseases (Total sample: 9165) in the dataset. Our study used 5 -fold stratified crossvalidation to assess TF-IDF vectorization, Bengali-specific preprocessing, and the traditional classifiers, Random Forest, SVM, Logistic Regression, and Naïve Bayes. The results of our study show that Random Forest performs better than other models, with an accuracy of 90.56%. The Random Forest's superior performance and ensemble approaches may improve classification accuracy for disease prediction based on symptoms. In this study, the feasibility of Bengali-language symptom classification for automated disease prediction is demonstrated, bridging the gap between AI-driven diagnostics and healthcare accessible to non-English speakers. In the future, research will look at word embedding, deep learning techniques, and hyperparameter optimization to further increase classification accuracy. This research contributes to the development of AI-powered medical devices for Bengali-speaking communities.

nodes.title: Evaluating surveillance systems to understand dengue burden in Bangladesh: a narrative review
nodes.authors: Tasnim Salam; Mst. Noorjahan Begum; Mustafizur Rahman
nodes.institutions: George Washington University; International Centre for Diarrhoeal Disease Research
nodes.subfield: Public Health, Environmental and Occupational Health
nodes.keywords: dengue; disease surveillance; Bangladesh; passive surveillance; active surveillance; outbreak forecasting; predictive modeling; early warning systems; data interoperability; underreporting; digital surveillance; outbreak preparedness and response
nodes.abstract: Abstract Dengue is an arboviral disease that clinically ranges from mild febrile illness to life-threatening hemorrhagic fever and shock syndrome. In Bangladesh, dengue incidence rose sharply over the past decade, culminating in the country’s largest outbreak in 2023. There are 321,179 confirmed cases and 1,705 deaths (case fatality rate: 0.53%) and the outbreak has not ended. Effective disease surveillance is essential for early outbreak detection, monitoring, and response. As the dengue burden continues to grow, the capacity of Bangladesh’s surveillance systems is increasingly constrained by challenges related to coordination, coverage, data integration, and insufficient funding. This narrative review synthesizes evidence from 20 peer-reviewed studies published between 2018 and 2024, using thematic analysis and an adapted PRISMA approach to examine existing dengue surveillance systems and identify opportunities to strengthen the capacity in Bangladesh. Two core surveillance modalities were identified, passive surveillance and active surveillance, supplemented by two predictive analytics approaches: forecasting and predictive modeling. Across these modalities, two primary surveillance approaches emerged: hospitalization and patient-record reporting, and community-level monitoring. Early warning systems were also identified within the forecasting and predictive modeling literature. Findings reveal substantial variability in data quality, timeliness, and interoperability across surveillance modalities and analytics tools. Passive and hospital-based reporting offer nationwide coverage but are limited by underreporting and delays, while active surveillance provides earlier signals yet lacks systematic integration with national platforms. Forecasting and predictive models show promise for anticipatory outbreak detection but require more robust validation and standardized data inputs. Overall, this review underscores the need for a more cohesive and integrated dengue surveillance architecture in Bangladesh. By strengthening data sharing, standardizing reporting practices, and adopting digital surveillance tools, public health systems could significantly enhance outbreak detection, preparedness, and response. Such an integrated system may also serve as a model for other dengue-endemic countries.

nodes.title: CulturalCrosswords: A Multilingual Benchmark of Answer Constraints and Grid Completion
nodes.authors: Isaac Saxton-Knight; Gabriel Saxton-Knight; Diego Oliveira; Tidor-Vlad Pricope; Aston Garratt; Jocelyn D'Arcy
nodes.keywords: crossword puzzles; multilingual benchmark; large language models; answer length
nodes.abstract: When several answers fit a riddle, exact-match scoring can penalise a valid response. CulturalCrosswords tests how answer constraints affect large language models (LLMs) solving cultural riddles, whose solutions draw on knowledge specific to a community. We constructed 53 crosswords from crowdsourced riddles in 42 languages and evaluated 11 LLM configurations on five versions of each clue set: plain batches, batches with lengths, batches with lengths and partial-answer hints, and crosswords requesting an answer list or a completed grid. On 962 clues with alternative answers, lengths improve agreement with the reference by 22.8 percentage points, compared with 8.4 points when accepted alternatives also receive credit. Part of the gain therefore appears to come from selecting a required answer form. Crossword input increases the share of all crossings with compatible answers by 9.7 points; requiring a completed grid reveals large differences between models. The benchmark distinguishes agreement with a reference from the ability to produce answers that fit together and occupy the correct cells.

nodes.title: Beyond Forgetting: Representation Misdirection Elicits Controllable Side Behaviors and Capabilities
nodes.authors: Tien Dang; The-Hai Nguyen; Dinh Mai Phuong; Nguyen Minh Phuong; Anh Bui; Hoang Thanh-Tung; Le-Minh Nguyen; Naoya Inoue
nodes.keywords: machine unlearning; large language models; linear representation hypothesis; latent representations; sentiment control; stereotypical bias; refusal behavior; in-context learning
nodes.abstract: We consider Representation Misdirection (RM), a class of large language model (LLM) unlearning methods that achieve forgetting by redirecting the latent representations of forget-samples toward a target vector. Despite being important, the roles of the target vector used in RM, however, remain underexplored. Here, we approach and revisit RM through the lens of the Linear Representation Hypothesis. Specifically, if one can identify a one-dimensional representation corresponding to a high-level concept, the Linear Representation Hypothesis enables linear operations on this concept vector within the forget-representation space. Under this view, we hypothesize that, beyond forgetting, machine unlearning via RM elicits controllable side effect behaviors and capabilities corresponding to the high-level concept. Our hypothesis is empirically validated across a wide range of concepts and tasks, including controlling unlearned models' truthfulness, sentiment, stereotypical bias, refusal, language, and in-context learning (ICL) tasks. Our findings reveal that this phenomenon could be either a hidden risk if misused or a mechanism that can be harnessed for developing unlearned models that require stronger capabilities and controllable behaviors.

nodes.title: BiRD: Bidirectional Residual Direction Steering of Strategic Social Decisions in LLMs
nodes.authors: Ivan Nasonov; Nikita Glazkov; Grigorii Bezotetskii; Mikhail Mozikov; A. Savchenko; Ilya Makarov
nodes.institutions: National Research University Higher School of Economics
nodes.keywords: large language models; strategic decision-making; bargaining; cooperation; trust; sparse autoencoders; refusal behavior; inference-time control
nodes.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly make strategic choices in bargaining, allocation, trust, and cooperation settings. We investigate whether additive interventions in residual activations can systematically modulate these decisions. We introduce BiRD (Bidirectional Residual Direction Steering), a valid-answer-aware protocol that constructs candidate directions from generic refusal, decision-derived, game-conditioned, and sparse-autoencoder contrasts, selects effective layers and intervention magnitudes, and evaluates them across six behavioral-economic games. Across six open-weight LLMs from four architecture families, BiRD identifies configurations that move decisions toward both more self-interested/non-cooperative and more generous/cooperative behavior. Repeated-generation analysis characterizes strong behavioral shifts and architecture-dependent validity trade-offs. At the same time, disjoint extraction, selection, and test contexts confirm both target orientations in all six models across five partitions. Primary-partition shifts reach + 0.562 and −0.373, and all twelve aggregate comparisons remain significant after multiplicity correction. Ablations and searched control directions establish the value of context-matched contrasts and model-specific intervention parameters. Frozen interventions also transfer to matched Russian prompts, while repeated interactions and independent human ratings characterize their practical scope. Together, these findings establish BiRD as a systematic framework for studying strategic decision-making through inference-time residual control.

nodes.keywords: open-source language models; multimodal reasoning; image understanding; audio understanding; mathematical reasoning; reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards; preference alignment; instruction following; document understanding; speech recognition; open data licensing
nodes.abstract: Language models are becoming infrastructure, and infrastructure built in the open, by public institutions, on documented data, is the alternative to dependence on a few providers; Apertus shows this is viable at scale. Apertus 1.5 extends the fully open Apertus family from text to multimodal reasoning. Continued pretraining of the Apertus 1.0 models, on 4T additional tokens for the 8B and 2T for the 70B, adds image and audio understanding and extends the context window fourfold to 262,144 tokens; multimodality enters through the tokenizer, the language-model head remains restricted to text, and the architecture is unchanged. Supervised finetuning, long-context finetuning, reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, and preference alignment complete the released models. Thinking is a flag of the chat template rather than a separate model, and lifts mathematical reasoning by up to 20 points on the 8B model. The released models improve over their predecessors on nearly every benchmark; among fully open models of its class, the 8B leads on knowledge, instruction following, and cultural benchmarks, and its instruction following surpasses all compared models, including open-weight ones. On image and audio understanding, a first for the family, the models are competitive with fully open multimodal models, strongest on document understanding and long-form and lower-resource speech recognition, while specialized vision and audio models remain ahead on perception and transcription of English and other high-resource languages. As in Apertus 1.0, we train only on openly available data, respect crawler opt-outs retroactively, and exclude restrictively licensed material. We release the model weights, data preparation and training recipes, and evaluation suites under permissive licenses; openness extends to values, with the Apertus charter guiding alignment stages published alongside the models.

nodes.title: HeRE: A Novel Benchmark for Hebrew Relation Extraction via LLM-Guided Denoising of Knowledge Graph Alignments
nodes.venue: International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing and Conference of the Asia-Pacific Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (IJCNLP-AACL)
nodes.authors: Ron Keinan; Amir David Nissan Cohen; Reut Tsarfaty
nodes.institutions: Bar-Ilan University
nodes.keywords: knowledge graph alignment; natural language inference; low-resource languages; multilingual LLMs; cross-training; few-shot learning
nodes.abstract: While LLMs demonstrate strong capabilities in English Relation Extraction (RE) tasks, a significant gap remains in assessing their RE performance in low-resource languages, due to a lack of standardized benchmarks.Creating native, language-specific annotated RE benchmarks is expensive and requires human expertise, while relying on translation yields suboptimal, inaccurate datasets that introduce Englishcentric biases.To tackle this, we propose a scalable, language-agnostic methodology to create RE data by denoising naturally occurring yet noisy alignments of knowledge bases and corresponding texts.We define a proper alignment via a Natural Language Inference (NLI) task, where a relation triplet is entailed by an input text.We empirically assess five denoising strategies, and demonstrate that multilingual models outperform language-specific models in the few-shot LLM setting, while Hebrewspecific encoders remain competitive under NLI fine-tuning and are strongest in the labelfree cross-training setting.We further find that prompting in the native language achieves performance on par with or slightly exceeding English prompts, confirming that the pipeline operates naturally in the target language.The best open-weights model, Gemma-4-31B-it (F1 = 0.915), matches the best API model, GPT-5.4 (0.921), and reaches F1 = 0.844 on a fully held-out, dual-annotated test set.Applying the optimized pipeline, we release HeRE: a novel, massive, 1.5-million-instance silver dataset for Hebrew RE, designed to support data-intensive experimentation and model fine-tuning.HeRE bridges a critical gap in standard Hebrew RE evaluation, while providing the NLP community with a reproducible, language-agnostic pipeline for RE dataset construction in other low-resource settings.
